title: Looking back
hook: stories, practices, portions, sayings, tales and songs: a year of Jewish life
tomorrow: year one close: the big lookout

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last line of the Book of Psalms. Your line was everything that breathes. Did a breath become a thank-you? Today, we stop and look back at the whole year. Day three hundred thirty.

When you climb a long hill, you mostly look down. At your feet, at the next step, at the rock you might trip on. It's only when you stop near the top and turn around that you see it: the whole path winding up behind you, the town tiny at the bottom, the place where you almost turned back. You didn't feel yourself climbing that far. But there it is. Today is that moment. We stop, turn around, and look at a year of Jewish life. Today: looking back.
screen: `EYES ON YOUR FEET.` → `STOP NEAR THE TOP AND TURN.` → `THE WHOLE PATH BEHIND YOU.`

segments.voice: The Torah itself does this. Near the end of the Book of Numbers, just before the Israelites reach the promised land, it stops and lists every place they camped in the wilderness. Forty-two stops, one after another. It could look like a boring list. But Rashi, the great commentator, passes on a parable. A king's son was sick, and his father took him far away to be healed. On the way home, the father pointed out each place: here we slept, here we were cold, here you had a headache. The list is love. It says: every stop counted. So let's name ours. We started with first words: shalom, the Shema, Shabbat, bracha, tzedakah, teshuvah. Then the stories: creation, Abraham, Jacob's long road, Joseph, the Exodus, the sea, Sinai. Then the practices: Shabbat candles, blessings through the day, the holidays as they came, tefillin, kashrut, study as prayer. Then the text, one portion at a time, from Bereshit into Exodus. And then the depths: the sayings of Pirkei Avot, be a mensch, don't judge until you've been there. A taste of Talmud: Hillel on one foot, Honi and his carob tree, these and these. The Hasidic tales: the shepherd boy's whistle, Zusya, the narrow bridge, the rebbe with the axe. And the Psalms, all the way to everything that breathes. You didn't feel yourself climbing this far. Some days you missed. Some days you only half listened. That's fine. The Torah lists the hard stops too. Look how far.
screen: `FORTY-TWO STOPS IN THE WILDERNESS.` · `HERE WE SLEPT, HERE WE WERE COLD.` · `WORDS, STORIES, PRACTICES, TEXT.` · `SAYINGS, TALES AND SONGS.` · then, large: `LOOK HOW FAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list five things you've kept. Settle, and breathe. Let the year play back. Don't try to remember everything. Let five things come up that stayed with you. A word. A story. A practice you actually do now. A line you've said to someone else. A moment that changed how you see something. Count them on your fingers, one by one. If you have paper nearby, write them down afterward. If you pray, you can give thanks for each one. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. The Torah stops before the promised land to name every place the people camped. Here we slept. Here we were cold. Every stop counted.
Your line: look how far. Today, tell one person one thing you've learned this year, and notice how far you've come to be able to say it. Day three hundred thirty.

howItsDone: The portion Masei, read each summer, lists all the Israelites' stops in the wilderness, and many Jews use the weeks before Rosh Hashanah to look back over the year that has passed.

fork.setup: the Israelites are about to enter the promised land after forty years. what does the Torah do first?
options: stop and list every place they camped.
tell them to forget the wilderness.
fork.reveal: Numbers 33 lists every stop. Rashi's parable: a father on the way home points out each place. here we slept, here we were cold.

original.note: Hebrew: the journeys of. The name of the portion that lists the wilderness stops (Numbers 33).

trapdoor: what you thought: a recap before the finale.
what it means: naming every stop, the good and the hard, is a way of honoring the whole journey.
what a scholar hears: Rashi on Numbers 33:1, drawing on Midrash Tanchuma, reads the list of forty-two stations as a father's loving recollection with a son who was healed on the way.

sources.ref: Rashi on Numbers 33:1 (from Midrash Tanchuma, Masei 3)
